1044.title: What the long story teaches
1044.hook: faith kept through exile, loss and renewal
1044.howItsDone: In the Ardas, said standing at the close of Sikh services and at other moments, the sangat remembers the Gurus and the Sikhs who gave their lives for their faith, and ends by asking for chardi kala through the Name and the good of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kitchen at Amritsar, and your line was tens of thousands fed. Did you serve someone first, or wash a plate that wasn't yours? Today, we step back from the kitchen and look at the whole year's road. Day one thousand forty-four.

Stand at the end of a long road and look back, and you can't see every step. You see the shape. A man with a musician beside him, walking from village to village. Towns built around a pool and a kitchen. Gurus who gave their lives rather than give way. A morning when five stood up. Hard years in the hills and forests. A kingdom won and lost. Marches with no weapons. A land split in two. A temple attacked, and grief in the streets. Families scattered across oceans, building gurdwaras in rented halls. All year, this path has walked that road. Today, what the long story teaches.
screen: `A MAN AND A MUSICIAN, WALKING.` → `MARTYRS, MARCHES, A LAND SPLIT.` → `GURDWARAS IN RENTED HALLS.`

segments.voice: First, the losses are real. This story doesn't pretend. There were Gurus tortured and killed, families driven from their homes, sacred places damaged, and friends who never came back. Sikhs don't hide those names. They say them out loud. Second, the remembering. In the Ardas, the prayer said standing at the close of Sikh services, the sangat recalls those who gave their lives and kept their faith: who were cut limb from limb, broken on wheels, sawn apart, and who kept their Sikhi with their uncut hair to the last breath. The losses are not forgotten. They're carried, standing, every day. Third, the renewal. After every hard chapter, something kept going. The Granth kept being read. The kitchen kept cooking. The gurdwara door kept opening, in a village in Punjab, a river town in Malaysia, a rented hall in a northern winter. Sikhs often tell it this way: the faith didn't go on by winning every fight, but by keeping its daily practices. Fourth, the spirit. The Ardas ends with this line: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. Through the Name, rising spirits, and by your will, the good of all. Chardi kala is the word for that spirit: rising, steady, even in loss. And notice what it asks for at the very end. Not victory. The good of all. That's today's line: the lesson of the story. As the Ardas holds it: remember everything, keep the practice, and keep asking good for everyone.
screen: `THE LOSSES ARE REAL.` · `THE ARDAS REMEMBERS THEM.` · `THE KITCHEN KEPT COOKING.` · `CHARDI KALA, AND THE GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `THE LESSON OF THE STORY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for the whole road. Sit, and let your breath slow. Let the year's stories pass in front of you like a slow train: the musician, the five, the marches, the kitchens. Don't hold any of them. Let one stop in front of you, the one that stayed with you most. Breathe in, and look at it. Breathe out, and name, quietly, one thing it taught you. Only one. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
What the long story teaches. A faith kept through exile, loss and renewal: remembering the losses, keeping the daily practice, and asking, in chardi kala, for the good of all. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT THE LONG STORY TEACHES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the lesson of the story. Today, write down the one lesson you named in the sit, in a single sentence, and put it somewhere you'll see it tomorrow. Day one thousand forty-four.

1045.title: Your family's story
1045.hook: every Sikh family carries part of this history
1045.howItsDone: Sikh families pass on the sakhis of the Gurus and their own histories by telling them aloud, and some families and Sikh groups record elders' memories of migration, partition and community life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what the long story teaches, and your line was the lesson of the story. Did you write your one lesson down? Today the long story comes home, to an older voice and one question. Day one thousand forty-five.

Where were you when you were my age? A boy asks it in the car on the way home from the gurdwara, mostly to fill the quiet. His grandfather, in the passenger seat, doesn't answer right away. Then he says the name of a village the boy has never heard. A well at the edge of it. A school two fields away. A morning when everyone packed what they could carry. The car pulls into the driveway, and the engine stops, and nobody reaches for the door. The story isn't finished yet. Today, your family's story.
screen: `WHERE WERE YOU AT MY AGE?` → `A VILLAGE HE'S NEVER HEARD OF.` → `NOBODY REACHES FOR THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, the big story lives in small ones. This year we've followed Gurus, marches, borders and ships. But the history doesn't sit only in books. Sikh families carry pieces of it: who crossed which border, who left a village, who drove a taxi through a first winter, who kept the Granth safe in a spare room. A family story is the long story at the size of one table. Second, the sakhi. Sikhs pass on the Gurus' own lives as sakhis, stories told aloud, often by elders to children. The family story belongs to that same habit: the past handed over by voice. Third, listening. In the Japji, at the opening Angs of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak gives a run of short verses to suniai, listening. Each one says what listening does: through listening, sorrow and wrongdoing are wiped away, and the devotees bloom. In Sikh practice, listening isn't only being polite. It's spiritual work. Fourth, how to ask. Some memories are sweet, and some hurt. A grandparent may laugh about a first job and go quiet about a border. So ask gently, ask one thing at a time, and let them decide how far to go. If they say no, that's an answer too. If they say yes, write it down, or ask to record it, because a story that lives in one voice can be lost. That's today's line: ask your elders. They're the archive no one else has.

segments.voice: Two minutes for the people who came before you. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind an elder: a grandparent, a parent, an old neighbor, a teacher, someone at the gurdwara or a place of worship you know. Picture their hands. Breathe in, and wonder what those hands have done that you've never heard about. Breathe out, and let one question form, the one you'd most like to ask them. Don't ask it yet. Just find it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Your family's story. The piece of the long history your own family carries, passed on by voice the way Sikhs pass on the sakhis, and kept by those who stop to listen. Today's word.
Your line: ask your elders. Today, ask one elder the question you found in the sit, and listen all the way to the end before you say anything. Day one thousand forty-five.

1046.title: Your place in the story
1046.hook: the story isn't over; you are part of what comes next
1046.howItsDone: Sikhs describe the daily life of a Sikh using passages such as Ang 305, where Guru Ram Das describes rising early, bathing and remembering the Name through the day, and they understand the Guru Granth Sahib and the Khalsa Panth as carrying the Gurus' work forward.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your family's story, and your line was ask your elders. Did you ask your question, and listen to the end? Today, the last page of this part of the long story, and the blank one after it. Day one thousand forty-six.

A notebook, written almost to the end. The last few lines are crowded: a kitchen on a highway, a turban explained at a table on a lawn, a river cleaned by hand, a forest on a scrap of dirt, a grandfather's story in a parked car. Then a page with nothing on it. Not torn out. Just waiting. That's where this part of the path has brought us, through the twentieth century and into today. The pen is on the table. Whose hand picks it up? Today, your place in the story.
screen: `A NOTEBOOK, NEARLY FULL.` → `THE CROWDED LAST LINES.` → `A BLANK PAGE, WAITING.`

segments.voice: First, the story isn't over. These last weeks weren't about the past. They were about Sikhs right now: in parliaments and at protests, in kitchens and classrooms, cleaning rivers, planting trees, arguing honestly about caste and about who may sing kirtan. Sikhs hold that the Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru and the Khalsa Panth carries the work on. That means the story keeps being written by ordinary people. Second, what an ordinary day looks like. At Ang 305, Guru Ram Das describes the one who calls himself a Sikh of the True Guru: rising early, bathing, remembering the Name, and keeping it through the day, sitting or standing, with every breath and every bite. Nothing in that list is grand. It's a day, done with attention. Third, the surprise at the end. The same hymn closes with Guru Ram Das, a Guru, asking for the dust of the feet of that kind of Sikh: the one who remembers the Name and helps others remember it too. The Guru bows to the ordinary day. Fourth, your place. Whether you're Sikh, learning about Sikhs, or here for someone you love, the story you've heard this year goes on through small acts. A plate washed. A question asked. A neighbor's turban understood. A promise kept. Tomorrow, the path turns to the calendar of memory, the days Sikhs gather to remember. Today, the line is simple: the story goes on.
screen: `SIKHS RIGHT NOW, NOT ONLY THEN.` · `ANG 305: AN ORDINARY DAY.` · `THE GURU ASKS FOR THE DUST.` · `SMALL ACTS CARRY IT ON.` · then, large: `THE STORY GOES ON.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the blank page. Sit, and let your breath slow. Picture that notebook, open to the empty page. Breathe in, and ask: what's one thing I could do today that would be worth telling someone, years from now? Not a big thing. Something true. Breathe out, and let one answer arrive. Don't judge it. Just see it on the page, in your own handwriting. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Your place in the story. The long story of the Sikhs isn't finished, and it keeps being written through ordinary days lived with attention, the kind of day Guru Ram Das honors. Today's word.
screen: `YOUR PLACE IN THE STORY — today's word`.

1047.title: Saka Nankana day
1047.hook: each February Sikhs remember the martyrs of Nankana, 1921
1047.howItsDone: On the yearly remembrance of Saka Nankana Sahib, gurdwaras hold kirtan and the Ardas in memory of the reformers, and pilgrims gather at Nankana Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your place in the story, and your line was the story goes on. Did you find one small way to carry it forward? Now the year turns to the days Sikhs keep on the calendar, so the story is never lost. Day one thousand forty-seven.

Not every day on the Sikh calendar is a birthday or a harvest fair. Some are kept for grief. One of them belongs to Nankana Sahib, the town tradition holds as Guru Nanak's birthplace. On a morning in the last century, reformers came to its gurdwara to pray, and were killed there without lifting a hand. This path has already walked through that morning. Sikhs still keep it on the calendar, and today's practice asks for something small: one lamp. Today: Saka Nankana day.
screen: `NOT A BIRTHDAY, NOT A FAIR.` → `A MORNING AT NANKANA.` → `ONE LAMP.`

segments.voice: This begins a new stretch of the path: the calendar of memory. How a people keeps grief says a lot about them. Start with the word. Sikhs call a remembered episode of martyrdom like this a saka. Saka Nankana is that morning, and the people it remembers are the reformers who walked into the gurdwara at Nankana Sahib, sat before the Guru Granth Sahib, and were attacked inside. You heard the full story earlier this year. Today, look at what the remembering holds up. These were not soldiers. Accounts say they had pledged not to strike back, and they kept the pledge. So the day doesn't remember a battle. It remembers a refusal: to answer violence with violence, even at the cost of their lives. Next, how the day is kept. There's kirtan, and there's the Ardas, the standing prayer that closes Sikh gatherings, which remembers those who gave their lives in service of the gurdwaras. Pilgrims gather at Nankana Sahib itself. Last, why it's kept this way. The Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib on Ang 1, names the One as nirbhau and nirvair: without fear, without enmity. That pair sits at the heart of the day. In the telling Sikhs keep, the reformers walked in without fear, and did not answer with enmity. So the day isn't kept with speeches against anyone. It's kept with a hymn and a prayer. That's today's line: the peaceful martyrs.
screen: `A CALENDAR OF MEMORY BEGINS.` · `A SAKA: A REMEMBERED MARTYRDOM.` · `KIRTAN, THE ARDAS, A LAMP.` · `WITHOUT FEAR, WITHOUT ENMITY.` · then, large: `THE PEACEFUL MARTYRS.`

segments.voice: Light a lamp for them. If you have a candle or a small lamp, and it's safe, light it now and set it where you can see it. If not, keep your eyes on any small light near you, a screen dimmed low, a window. Let the flame stand for people who came to pray and did not strike back. You don't need to see the morning itself. Just keep the light company. Breathe slowly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. Two words to rest on: without fear, without enmity. The bell holds the time.
Saka Nankana day. The day each year when Sikhs remember the reformers killed at Nankana Sahib, who had pledged not to strike back. Today's word.
Your line: the peaceful martyrs. Today, when something provokes you, let it pass once without answering in kind. Nobody needs to know why. Day one thousand forty-seven.

1048.title: Saragarhi Day
1048.hook: every 12 September the twenty-one are remembered
1048.howItsDone: On Saragarhi Day, the Sikh Regiment of the Indian Army and Sikh gatherings elsewhere remember the soldiers of Saragarhi, often by reading their names, with Ardas and a moment of silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saka Nankana day, and your line was the peaceful martyrs. Did something provoke you, and did you let it pass? Today's day of memory is about soldiers, and it's kept in a very different way. Day one thousand forty-eight.

The little post at Saragarhi talked to the world with a mirror and the sun: flashes of light sent from one fort to another across the ridge. Earlier on this path you heard how the signals kept coming on the day the post was surrounded, and how the men inside stayed. Now the post is gone. What's left is a day on the calendar. On Saragarhi Day, in regimental halls, in gurdwaras and in homes, someone reads out a list of names, and people stand still while it's read. Today: Saragarhi Day.
screen: `A MIRROR AND THE SUN.` → `THE POST IS GONE.` → `A LIST OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: First, the story in one breath. Sikh soldiers of a British Indian regiment held a small signal post called Saragarhi, under Havildar Ishar Singh. A much larger force surrounded it. They held on, Sikh memory says, until the last of them had fallen. That memory counts them: twenty-one. Second, how the day is kept. It's kept by name. The Sikh Regiment of the Indian Army marks Saragarhi Day, and so do Sikh gatherings far beyond it. A roll is read. Havildar Ishar Singh. The signaler, Gurmukh Singh. And the rest, one at a time. A number like twenty-one is easy to say and easy to forget. Names are harder to forget. Each name is a person who stayed. Third, a verse Sikhs often bring to days like this. In a salok of Bhagat Kabir in the Guru Granth Sahib, on Ang 1105, Kabir says, in paraphrase, that the true hero is the one who fights for the helpless, and who, though cut to pieces, never leaves the field. Some Sikh teachers read Kabir first as speaking of the inner battle, the fight with one's own fear and greed. But the picture of someone who won't leave the field is why his salok is heard on a day like this. Fourth, the honest part. The men who attacked the post were fighting for their own valleys and homes. The day isn't kept against them. It's kept for twenty-one people, and for the plain fact that they stayed. That's today's line: twenty-one.
screen: `A SMALL POST, AND THEY STAYED.` · `THE DAY IS KEPT BY NAME.` · `KABIR: HE NEVER LEAVES THE FIELD.` · `NOT KEPT AGAINST ANYONE.` · then, large: `TWENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Stand still for twenty-one seconds. If you're able, stand up. Feet planted, hands at your sides, eyes soft. Count slowly in your head, one second for each of the twenty-one. You don't need to know their names. Let each count be one person. When you reach twenty-one, sit down again and breathe. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. If you don't, just let the stillness be your way of honoring them. Then rest, and let the breath steady itself. The bell holds the time.
Saragarhi Day. The day each year when the soldiers of the post at Saragarhi are remembered by name. Today's word.
Your line: twenty-one. Today, learn one name you usually skip past: the guard at your building, the person who cleans your office, a neighbor. Say it out loud next time. Day one thousand forty-eight.

1049.title: The thirteenth of April
1049.howItsDone: On Vaisakhi, people visit the Jallianwala Bagh memorial in Amritsar to remember those killed there, while the city also celebrates the harvest and the birth of the Khalsa. Some gurdwaras include the memory of the garden in their Vaisakhi gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saragarhi Day, and your line was twenty-one. Did you learn one name you usually skip past? Today, a day of memory that shares its date with a festival. Day one thousand forty-nine.

How do you keep a festival and a funeral on the same day? In Amritsar, that isn't a riddle. It's the calendar. In the morning, the city fills for Vaisakhi: the harvest is in, the Khalsa's birthday is sung, there's langar and color and noise. And a short walk from the Harmandir Sahib there's a walled garden where, on a Vaisakhi long ago, troops fired into an unarmed crowd. People come to that garden on the same day, quietly. Today: the thirteenth of April.
screen: `A FESTIVAL AND A FUNERAL?` → `VAISAKHI IN AMRITSAR.` → `A WALLED GARDEN.`

segments.voice: Earlier this path told the story of Jallianwala Bagh, and later the long memory of Udham Singh. Today isn't the story again. It's what the date now carries. First, one date, two memories. The firing at Jallianwala Bagh happened on Vaisakhi day. So ever since, Vaisakhi in Punjab has held a second memory inside the first. Some celebrate in the morning and remember in the afternoon, and the two sit side by side. Second, who was there. The crowd in the garden was Sikh, Hindu and Muslim together, some of them visitors in town for the festival. So the memory doesn't belong to one community. People of different faiths come to the garden to remember. Third, the place itself. The garden is a memorial now. Visitors see the marks in the walls and the well, and some lower their voices without being told. A place can teach silence on its own. Fourth, a line from the Guru Granth Sahib that fits a mixed crowd. On Ang 1299, Guru Arjan sings, in paraphrase, that no one is my enemy and no one is a stranger; I get along with all. Some Sikhs hold that line beside the garden, because the people who died there were strangers to each other and are remembered together. And it's a guard against the easy road from grief to hatred. Remembering the garden doesn't mean making enemies of anyone living today. So the festival isn't spoiled by the memory, and the memory isn't drowned by the festival. That's today's line: vaisakhi remembers.
screen: `ONE DATE, TWO MEMORIES.` · `A CROWD OF SEVERAL FAITHS.` · `THE GARDEN TEACHES SILENCE.` · `NO ONE IS MY ENEMY.` · then, large: `VAISAKHI REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: One minute of silence. Sit, or stand if you'd rather. Let your hands rest. For one minute, say nothing and do nothing. No phone, no plans. Let the silence be for the people in the garden: Sikh, Hindu and Muslim, visitors and neighbors, who came for a festival. No need to picture what happened. Let the silence be enough. When the minute feels done, breathe slowly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. Then rest in the quiet a little longer. The bell holds the time.
The thirteenth of April. A Vaisakhi date that also holds the memory of Jallianwala Bagh, where an unarmed crowd of several faiths was fired on. Today's word.
Your line: vaisakhi remembers. Today, if you're celebrating anything, even a small win, pause for one breath to remember someone who can't celebrate with you. Day one thousand forty-nine.

1050.title: The great holocaust remembered
1050.hook: Sikhs gather at Kup Rahira to remember 1762
1050.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Vadda Ghallughara with Ardas and kirtan in gurdwaras, and some gather at Kup Rahira, where the families were caught, to remember those who died there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the thirteenth of April, and your line was vaisakhi remembers. Did you pause for someone who couldn't celebrate with you? Today, a day of memory with a hard name. Day one thousand fifty.

Flat fields, two villages, a road between them. On an ordinary day, the ground holds crops. But on the day of remembrance, cars and buses pull in, and Sikhs walk out across the fields toward a memorial at Kup Rahira. Families come together: grandparents, parents, small children on shoulders. That's fitting, because what happened here happened to families. Sikhs call it the Vadda Ghallughara, the great holocaust. This path has told the day itself. Today: the great holocaust remembered.
screen: `FLAT FIELDS, TWO VILLAGES.` → `FAMILIES WALK OUT TOGETHER.` → `THE VADDA GHALLUGHARA.`

segments.voice: First, what the gathering remembers. A slow column of Sikh families, the old and the young, was caught in the open by Ahmad Shah Abdali's army. The fighters with them formed a ring and kept the column moving, fighting on the outside. The losses were terrible, and the old accounts don't agree on how many died. The remembrance doesn't turn on a figure. It turns on the people. Second, who is at the center. You might expect a war memory to put soldiers in the middle. This one, in Sikh memory, puts the families there: the mothers, the children, the elders in the carts. The fighters are honored for one thing above all: they stayed between the danger and the ones who couldn't run. Third, a hymn that draws the same shape. On Ang 819, Guru Arjan sings, in paraphrase, that the hot wind does not touch the one who is under the Lord's shelter, and that all around is drawn the Lord's protecting circle, so pain cannot come near. The hymn is about the shelter of the Name, not about a battle. But a circle drawn around the vulnerable is the same picture the accounts of that day leave. Fourth, the week. This week looked at what the long story teaches, your family's story, and your place in it. Then the calendar of memory began: reformers who did not strike back at Nankana, twenty-one names at Saragarhi, a garden at Vaisakhi, and now this field. Each day is kept with prayer and names, not with hatred for anyone living. That's today's line: they shielded the families.
screen: `A COLUMN CAUGHT IN THE OPEN.` · `THE FAMILIES AT THE CENTER.` · `A PROTECTING CIRCLE, ANG 819.` · `A WEEK OF DAYS OF MEMORY.` · then, large: `THEY SHIELDED THE FAMILIES.`

segments.voice: Pray for families, or hold them in mind. Sit comfortably and breathe. Bring to mind one family you know: your own, a neighbor's, a friend's. Then let the circle widen to families anywhere who are on the move, or in danger, or simply worn out. Don't try to fix anything. Just keep them inside the circle for a while. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them, or hold the line from Ang 819 in your heart. If you don't, simply wish them shelter. The bell holds the time.
The great holocaust remembered. The day Sikhs gather at Kup Rahira for the families caught in the open, and for those who formed a ring around them. Today's word.
Your line: they shielded the families. Today, stand between someone and a small harm: take the late shift, walk someone home, step in when a child is being teased. Day one thousand fifty.
